blocks.text: Clinical pearl: A patient with major trauma and shock may have no visible external bleeding. Always search for concealed blood loss in the chest, abdomen, pelvis, retroperitoneum and long bones.
The traditional ATLS classification uses four classes of haemorrhage.
Remember that hypotension is a late sign of haemorrhagic shock, particularly in children.

items.text: Class I: Mild blood loss, usually compensated.
Class II: Moderate blood loss, tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction.
Class III: Severe blood loss with hypotension and significant perfusion impairment.
Class IV: Life-threatening blood loss with profound circulatory compromise.

blocks.text: Children may maintain blood pressure despite substantial blood loss because of strong compensatory mechanisms.
Clinical pearl: Do not wait for hypotension before recognising and treating paediatric haemorrhagic shock.

blocks.text: B. Paediatric Lund and Browder chart
Children have proportionally larger heads and smaller lower limbs compared with adults. The Lund and Browder chart is preferred for accurate paediatric TBSA estimation.
Clinical pearl: Only partial-thickness and full-thickness burns are included when calculating TBSA for fluid resuscitation. Superficial erythema-only burns are excluded.

Clinical pearl: Facial burns, singed nasal hairs, soot in the mouth, hoarseness and enclosed-space exposure should raise suspicion of inhalational injury. Early specialist airway assessment is essential.
The traditional formula estimates the initial 24-hour fluid requirement using lactated Ringer's solution.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: The definitive treatment for uncontrolled traumatic haemorrhage is haemorrhage control. Resuscitation must proceed alongside operative, endovascular or other definitive intervention rather than delaying it.
